Utilizing $6.0$ years of data collected by the LHC experiment, researchers analyzed the $\missingp$ signal for the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ transformation to determine the $B^0_s$ average lifetime. By refining the signal projection method and focusing on the time-dependent $K^+K^-$ mass spectrum, the $B^0_s$ lifetime was calculated. Initially, with no additional constraints, the $\Gamma B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ width was found to be $(0.50\pm0.12\pm0.10)\text{ ps}$, which can be converted to the $B^0_s$ lifetime of $(1.16\pm0.26\pm0.21)\text{ ps}$. Alternatively, using an external value for the $B^0_s$ natural width, the $B^0_s$ lifetime was also determined to be $(1.16\pm0.10\pm0.09)\text{ ps}$.

The control problem's discretization method is examined, where the underlying process follows a random differential equation. It is shown that a specific discretization of this control problem is equivalent to a quadratic form that results from its perturbed version. Furthermore, the relationship between the original control problem and its quadratic form is represented using an operator related to its pseudo-inverse. These findings are useful in proving convergence theorems for numerical methods used to solve and understand the characteristics of this random differential equation.

At the Pierre Auger Observatory, extensive air shower events exceeding 4 EeV in energy were analyzed to investigate the extent of high-energy cosmic-ray anisotropies. A study of the angular distribution of cosmic showers, detected as triples of scintillator arrays, was conducted to identify any patterns of local or large-scale anisotropy. To quantify the degree of anisotropy in different directions, we employed multiple metrics, taking into consideration the varying sensitivity of different parts of the detector. A particular year with exceptional annual exposure was selected for in-depth examination of the extensive anisotropy patterns exhibited by recorded high-energy cosmic showers. During this period, the dominant anisotropy source was found to be situated approximately 240 degrees opposite the Centaurus constellation and possessed an upper limit of 4% (90% confidence level), with this position's anisotropy extent being significantly more measurable than in any other direction on the sky.
This paper provides a proof that zinbiel algebras are strictly nilpotent, thereby confirming a conjecture proposed by Loday in 2012.

The paper investigates the anisotropic flow of lead-lead particles produced in LHC's high-energy collisions, specifically investigating the relationship between particle multiplicity and anisotropic flow, and the influence of initial conditions on this relationship. By utilizing the PHENIX team's data from the Pb-Pb 5.02 TeV collisions, and employing the $v_n$ multiplicity correlation function and the $v_n-\langle v_n\rangle$ separation function, the research reveals that higher-order anisotropic flow, particularly plane, is influenced by particle multiplicity, with a range of initial conditions explored through a thermodynamic model. The results obtained are comparable to those from the LHC for Pb-Pb collisions at the same energy level, albeit with differing interpretations, and also present initial conditions for smaller systems such as Au-Au collisions at lower energy levels.

This work focuses on resolving inconsistencies in table data, specifically addressing two unique challenges not commonly found in other research. Firstly, it deals with null values that lack a specific meaning in table cells. Unlike other studies, where null values can represent various unknown aspects, this study assumes they simply mean missing information pertaining to the relation's attribute. Secondly, it deals with functional dependencies, where a particular column or group of columns can be used to predict another column or group of columns within the table. Existing methods do not apply in this scenario. A proposed solution is an efficient and effective set of algorithms to detect and correct inapplicable values that contradict functional dependencies, considering the possible scenarios when a target value is either an individual attribute or an entire relation projected on some attributes or when an determinant relation is projected on some attributes or an entire relation. The proposed methods are validated using a database of 10,000 synthetic relations and real-world datasets consisting of 500 CSV files. The results demonstrate that the proposed techniques successfully address inconsistencies in tables with functional dependencies and null values.

Linear Gaussian time series models, such as the autoregressive (AR) and periodic autoregressive (PAR) models, are well-established statistical tools. Non-linear and periodic non-linear statistics models offer significant advantages over their linear counterparts in modeling. In this research, we introduce a non-linear periodic statistics model called the Poisson autoregressive model with seasonal variation of coefficients (PARMAC). This new model extends existing Poisson autoregressive models by allowing for the examination of seasonal variations in model coefficients. We outline the PACMAC model's methodology and inference in detail, outlining its mathematical framework. To further illustrate the efficacy of the PACMAC model in real-world data modeling, we present simulation studies along with an application.

Recent advancements in object representation learning have focused on compact, task-oriented objects for specific functions like natural language interaction and autonomous operation. These options, however, fall short when dealing with spatial relationships and operations requiring a deeper understanding of an object's position in 3D space. This work introduces Neural Description Fields (NDFs), a novel class of object representations that offer a unified, equvariant description of an object's local features, global orientation, and a condensed, latent space embedding. By leveraging their inherent potential, NDFs can perform diverse tasks, including object recognition, reconstruction, and interaction with minimal retraining. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NDFs in object description, instance segmentation, and finding lost objects, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods in the aforementioned tasks.

The precise classification of the Atkin-Lehner-Fukuda (ALFU) universality class, which describes the long-range behavior of neutral Higgs bosons in the Standard Model, along with other ALFU-based universality classes in particle physics, remains an unresolved issue. To address this problem, a Monte Carlo simulation was conducted to calculate density correlation functions and determine the global structural properties of large matrices representing two-point correlation functions. These calculations yielded two key parameters that, when plotted on phase diagrams, reveal distinct regions corresponding to various universality classes. When these regions are compared, the parameters align with existing classifications, including the ALFU class near the boundary of the non-zero-solution region for complex parameter space. Calculations for two models with Sp(4s) and SU(2s) symmetries in the ALFU class, as well as the Yang-Lee edge critical point, were also included in this analysis.

In statistics and machine learning, basic convex optimization is often insufficient, and even moderately "local" convexity is sometimes not adequate. This issue is clearly illustrated by the analysis of the approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. As it stands, an effective local analysis technique for AMP, developed by De Saade, Ben David, and Montanari, reveals only "local" convexity of the relevant free energy landscape, a property that closely relates to the approximation of certain physical phenomena. However, the type of convexity identified in this study is highly probable to be mistaken for an inherent property of the landscape, which could potentially lead to misinterpretation, since a more thorough analysis would likely show it is merely a reflection of deforming an entirely flat landscape. We argue that by modifying the algorithm's analysis technique to incorporate an explicit Sudakov-Fernique comparison step, one could instead demonstrate "post-AMP" local convexity, thereby showing that the approximate message passing (TAP) algorithm's examination area features explicit local convexity in relation to a completely neutral landscape. The implementation of this new approach also yields additional results, specifically demonstrating the same type of convexity in the Motzkin-Speyer state evolution framework.

Recent changes in optical stellar light patterns have been utilized to detect and assess atmospheric aerosols, with comparisons made to conventional methods demonstrating the value of this new approach, especially in assessing high-altitude aerosols. This handwriting-style summary incorporates two key findings: one research article's demonstration of using changes in colored star images to develop atmospheric models and another team's use of high-resolution CCD data for high-altitude aerosol assessment over Delhi, India - showing vertical distributions that differ significantly between Delhi and Alexandria, Egypt due to their geographic locations.

Recently, researchers have successfully utilized correspondence loss to enhance the accuracy of human pose estimation. This study builds upon this foundation by addressing the limitations of current clustering-based methods, which struggle to effectively incorporate semantic information due to their simplified distance metrics. To overcome these constraints, we introduce our novel DeepHMap++ framework, which replaces the traditional linear projection in these methods with a two-stage nonlinear projection network composed of a projection encoder and a clustering module. Furthermore, we incorporate the correspondence loss into the training process to enhance semantic feature learning. Through comparative experiments on two benchmark datasets, MIT and BNC, our model demonstrates superior performance over nine state-of-the-art approaches, achieving a 6% and 10% reduction in average error rates on the BNC and MIT datasets, respectively.

Python is a widely used tool for scientific calculations and visualizations due to its simplicity, which has led to the development of numerous Python-based numerical libraries. However, there are only limited Python libraries dedicated to advanced statistics and optimization problems, including the Graphical Lasso. The Graphical Lasso, a maximum likelihood estimation method, recovers a conditional independence graph from multivariate Gaussian data and has been extensively studied and applied in fields like finance, neuroscience, and genomics. Since the BIC criterion for graph reconstruction was recently introduced, the increasing interest in this approach has resulted in a surge of research and applied studies, necessitating a Python library for BIC calculation and graph reconstruction. GGLasso, a new Python library, is designed to compute BIC values for a range of graph structures, produces the best independence graph according to the BIC criterion, performs standard Graphical Lasso estimation using Tweedie's 2019 implementation, and provides a comprehensive set of tools and documentation including examples, tutorials, and TWA tests to ensure the library's reliability.

In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of using molecular dynamics simulations to determine the equilibrium configuration of molecules under various conditions, specifically during the Langevin dynamics process. Our analysis reveals the statistical methods suitable for assessing structural stability over time and evaluates their reliability in ensuring accurate representation of molecular arrangements. Furthermore, we propose novel diagnostic approaches, drawing on autocorrelation analysis and reverse-time simulation techniques to assess the reliability and accuracy of time-resolved molecular structures. These methods are examined in detail through actual and simulated test cases, providing valuable insights into improving the quality of molecular structure sampling.

In recent years, network analysis has expanded to include multi-layered systems across various fields, yet node promotion methods mostly remain adapted from traditional single-layer network approaches. We developed a novel node prominence metric specifically tailored for multi-layered networks called Eigenvector Prominance Multi-layer (EPM), taking into consideration the interconnected nature of network layers. Unlike traditional methods that treat each layer independently, we believe the relationships between layers should be considered to provide a more precise promotion assessment. We integrated a statistical model called Hidden Markov Random Walk (HMRW) to evaluate node prominence across connected network layers. Our approach demonstrated superior performance compared to existing methods through extensive simulations and real-world applications.

In 1935, Dirac formulated an expression for the area enclosed by a loop in spacetime that relied on the gauge-invariant field strength tensor, forming the basis for the subsequent Yang-Mills and Einstein equations. Nearly nine decades later, we have managed to recreate this formulation using classical phase-space variables, where the details of spacetime geometry significantly influence the results. Our reproduction of Dirac's original equation varies depending on whether the underlying spacetime has two, three, or more dimensions. In spacetimes with four angles, our expression for the area enclosed by a loop is found to be directly related to the Yang-Mills functional, whereas it is equivalent to the total energy within a region of spacetimes with three angles and to the total momentum within the area enclosed by a loop in spacetimes with two angles.

When spheres move through fluids and hit surfaces, they can cause damage upon entry as solids or as liquids which affects shaping and potential applications of the spheres. This study delves into the surface seal breaking phenomenon that occurs when spheres are filled with fluid and plunged into the same substance externally. It examines the conditions under which spheres retain a layer of fluid beneath them, also known as the pocket, and when this pocket breaks, affecting potential applications. By analyzing different pocket sizes, impact speeds, depths, sphere sizes, and fluid viscosities, we developed an approach to predict pocket formation and duration. In our investigation of four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ effective field theories with maximally realized symmetries, we found an expanded set of parameters that define theta-angles after symmetries are broken. This set is significantly larger than previously thought, growing in proportion to the number of independent channels through which nonperturbative effects vary. We then explored how the axion-dilaton fields influence the theta-terms produced, as well as the impact of instanton effects on the set of parameters. Furthermore, we examined the relationship between our findings and the behavior of axion dark matter.

Our theoretical investigation reveals that cubanite CuFe2S3 exhibits significant structural stability, with a -46.16 eV per atom total energy value, and shows cubic symmetry in accordance with its actual mineralogical properties. Our findings indicate that cubanite displays metal-like characteristics and weak spontaneous magnetization, alongside intricate orbital ordering, where iron's 3d electrons occupy three distinct energy levels filled by specific d-orbitals on opposite crystallographic planes, while demonstrating antiphase patterns within parallel planes and antiferromagnetic ordering between them, thereby explaining the mineral's antiferromagnetic nature and other magnetic properties, despite the small, negligible magnitude of these features.

The intricate behavior of the self-trapped dark exciton in $a$-SiN$_x$ is investigated under various temperatures and doping levels through detailed experiments and simulations. Our research reveals that a natural radiation process from dark to bright states occurs without the need for an external magnetic field, and under an 8T magnetic field, we observed the expected dark to bright state splitting of 11.4 meV as predicted by theory. The magnitude of this splitting matched the theoretical model, and we successfully measured the dark exciton magnetic g-factor for the first time. Furthermore, our studies enabled us to calculate the dark exciton radiative lifetime for the first time, and we found it to be approximately 1.12, 2.04, and 3.21 seconds for temperatures of 4.2 K, 77 K, and 300 K, respectively.

Two-dimensional electron lattice structures are classified into 17 distinct wallpaper groups based on their symmetry. Recent advances have discovered that certain conditions can increase this number to 23 by incorporating diagonal mirror lines, and further to 34 by adding tri-fold rotational axes. In this research, we investigate the symmetry-based electronic properties of these enhanced lattices and, using the Kane-Cooper method, create symmetries-based lattice models to analyze how their symmetry dictates features at specific points in space. We demonstrate that certain points in these lattices possess unique characteristics, known as Kammereyer points, which possess specific mathematical properties that can be traced back to the underlying lattice structure. By applying lattice distortions and the introduction of patterns that vary across space, we show that interesting behaviors, rooted in symmetry, can emerge in these lattice structures. Through computational simulations, we show how these behaviors disappear when the variations in patterns are reduced. Finally, we establish a theoretical framework that explains the unique properties that can be observed in these lattice structures at specific points in space.

Quantum states exhibiting intrinsic coherent superpositions, such as the Schrödinger cat states with their inherent phase symmetry, are highly valuable for advancing quantum technologies. However, generating these states is an intricate and costly process, often involving complicated multi-photon processes. Quantum-optical catalysis, a singular-photon mediated process, offers a novel approach to producing intrinsic phase-symmetric multi-photon components on its own. We propose using single-photon catalysis to generate a new type of cat state called the single-photon facilitated coherent (SPFC) state. Taking advantage of the catalysis' information gain, we further developed a scheme to convert the SPFC state into a desired cat state in both linear and non-linear setups. This conversion process can be extremely efficient and highly selective, paving the way for efficient cat-state-based quantum applications.

In General Relativity, using the Newman-Penrose framework, we explore the bivector formalism and demonstrate the direct linearity relationship between the four Newman-Penrose scalar components and the five independent components of the Weyl curvature in both vacuum and non-vacuum scenarios.

Using deductive frameworks, our goal is to establish the solution to systems of equations representing ordinary and linear polymers. These systems, when given specific parameters, can be utilized for predictive purposes. In our research, the systems were simplified using Python's whole programming framework, demonstrating their ability to find solutions on their own. The systems' predictive capability also allows for solutions to be obtained even without full knowledge of the underlying graph structure. Additionally, we explored the connection between linear and ordinary polymers, discovering that linear operators can be employed to translate between the two.

Segmenting tumors in the esophagus using CT scans is still challenging due to
several difficulties, including low contrast, irregular borders, and the esophagus'
similar appearance to surrounding tissues. Researchers have attempted to resolve
this issue through various techniques, such as advanced edge detection, dense
unets, and feature extraction, but it remains problematic. This study introduces
the DDAUnet model, which combines a dense unet framework with additional diluted
units to create larger receptive fields, allowing the network to process larger
segments more effectively. The DDAUnet model consists of three key components: an
enhanced receptive field module, which uses different units to capture local and
global features, the standard dense unet framework, which captures mid-level features,
and the multi-decoding multi-dilation module, which increases the segment's size
while capturing local and global segments. This model was trained using the RETNA
dataset and achieved an overall Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.732, which
is comparable to other leading methods but difficult to compare directly due to
the lack of standardized metrics and the irregular nature of the esophagus' tumor
segments.

The benefits of artificial intelligence and the widespread use of the internet have led to an explosion of text-based content, yet the limited availability of curated data has hindered the development of robust, open-source machine learning models. To address this challenge, domain-adaptive models were introduced, requiring the collaboration of diverse stakeholders to gather and clean vast amounts of content, exemplified by community-driven platforms such as Wikipedia, Wikipedia2OPUS, and GitHub. Despite their success, these platforms are plagued by inconsistencies and errors due to their heterogeneous nature, complicating the creation of high-quality, annotated datasets. To study the feasibility of developing such datasets through code-switching NLP techniques, we conducted experiments using a controlled, real-world dataset that incorporates code-switches and various influencing factors. However, the potential limitations of code-switching NLP annotation are likely to restrict its practical applications. As a result, the practical use of these models and platforms may require alternative data annotation methods without the use of code-switching.

As multiple human-centric evaluation methods for AI systems have humans providing feedback, it is reasonable to question why we aren't using them for creating and assessing automatic image captioning. This paper explores the reasons behind not employing human references for this purpose and puts out both theoretical and practical arguments, including an experiment to back them up. To do the experiment, we converted human feedback from a published paper's dataset into automatically generated descriptions and assessed the resulting model against this new benchmark using various comparison techniques. Our evaluation showed that the current prevailing assessment using rank-based algorithms lags significantly behind human performance, while our argument is supported by an equalization of the results with actual human accuracy. Despite not surpassing it, this striking discrepancy between the current assessment and what we expect from the best possible ranking was not previously noticed and was not using the best available techniques to create the model. This unexplored issue, in my opinion, points to the need for novel approaches in research that are centered around the human element.

Tantalum pentoxide, an electrically insulating material, exhibits remarkable dielectric properties and experiences unusual phase transformations when subjected to extreme pressures, with distinct characteristics pertinent to advanced capacitor technology and planetary geology. Despite its interest, the pressure-induced crystal structure of tantalum pentoxide remains unknown. By examining various possible crystal configurations, we discovered that its high-pressure state could be either the gamma or delta form. To investigate in detail, we studied how electrons behave, how taatalum atoms move, and observed how these actions change the crystal's density and electronic conductance, as well as its compression, thermal, and electrical conductive properties. Our studies showed that pressure could cause a switch in the crystal configuration, with a sudden change in how electrons behave, and also altered the material's compression, thermal, and conductive properties. In addition, we observed that the crystal configuration with the most stable and compact form was likely the delta form, with a new, highly stable configuration with electrons moving freely around its atoms, just before it underwent a sudden change into another form at very high pressures. Furthermore, we found that this new form had similar characteristics to another possible crystal configuration, with a more open structure, in a sudden change of form into another configuration with electrons moving around its tightly packed atoms. Lastly, we studied how temperature influenced the material's behavior, with a point of no return beyond which the form with the most stable and compact form disappeared, with the other form taking its place.

Previous research indicates that spatial information can influence the spread of misinformation among online users. However, extensive studies focusing on the significant impact of geographic information on misinformation dissemination within large-scale online communities remain uncommon. In this paper, a probable mechanism is proposed to explain how geographic information influences the spread of misinformation. A Bayesian Protopic Deep Tensor Factorization (BPDTF) model was employed to validate this assumption and gather further insights. By utilizing 435 million comments from 285 subreddits in Reddit.com during a one-year period (2018), evidence was obtained to support the hypothesis that spatial information plays a crucial role in determining the discourse of online users across large-scale communities. Furthermore, by examining U.S. Reddit communities in conjunction with an integrated knowledge graph, valuable side findings were discovered by analyzing U.S. state abbreviations' meanings, the implications of misinformation advertisements, the association between misinformation and political discussions, and the sources of misinformation. These insights provide actionable recommendations for content moderation strategies and defensive measures against misinformation dissemination. Furthermore, this research enriches the current body of knowledge by combining the generalizations of spatial information with social network analysis. As a result, geographical information is referred to as "big geographic information," and our research model offers valuable implications for further applications in the analysis of large-scale spatial data within online communities.

Verbal guidance from human instructors has significantly contributed to the development of robust robotic systems capable of performing intricate tasks. Yet, to date, there is limited understanding of the speech patterns employed by instructors when teaching social robots, taking into account the fact that speech comprehension relies on a different set of principles compared to human learning. To address this knowledge gap and incorporate a more realistic approach to teaching social robots, this study aims to establish comprehensive human instructions speech patterns associated with specific manipulation activities. Through the analysis of audio recordings and corresponding video footage, we identified and correlated acoustic speech patterns with specific manipulation activities performed by instructors using a computer interface. The findings reveal that incorporating human instructions speech patterns can serve as an effective tool for classifying specific manipulation activities automatically. To further validate this result, we developed a machine learning-based approach to classify the activities using only audio input. Overall, this study provides foundational knowledge for the development of advanced robotic systems that can be taught through verbal instructions.

This research examines the fundamental theory of geometric field moments in contrast to classic analogues. In particular, we investigate how Euler-Arnold equations drive field moments' intricacy and facilitate a deeper understanding of non-linear interactions stemming from quadratic advection terms. Furthermore, we introduce a set of local and non-local closure approximations aimed at resolving these equations. Additionally, a revised framework for incorporating metrics into dynamical systems is explored, enabling the development of gravitational field theories from archimedean invariance within a broad parameter space. As a concrete example, we illustrate how this approach can yield the Einstein field equations.

The escalating demand for conversational agents in various sectors such as healthcare, finance, and education has made their successful deployment crucial. Despite the potential of conversational bots to accomplish tasks effectively, many users find them difficult to use. To address this issue, usability testing has been established as a vital evaluation method. However, the current available protocols often lack consistency and reliability due to the subjective assessments made by human evaluators. This problem is exacerbated during the initial stages of the development process, where comprehensive system modifications are costly and time-consuming. This paper introduces the Conversational Usability Framework (CUF), an innovative approach to usability testing that integrates automated evaluation, achieving high consistency and reliability. The framework has been successfully applied to a real-world conversational agent used at a university, and the resulting data highlights areas of difficulty users encounter during system navigation. Additionally, the framework's effectiveness has been demonstrated in a case study, and the resulting usability issues it identifies align with those identified using the SUS protocol. The source code for the framework is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/a-shivam/cuf-framework.

Recent years have seen the rapid expansion of online shopping, fuelled by
the widespread adoption of the internet and social media. As the amount of
product information and customer reviews grows, customers are increasingly
overwhelmed and in need of effective recommendation systems to guide their
browsings. In a typical scenario, customers' preferences are shaped by both
their general tastes and specific interests in particular product aspects,
however, existing recommendation systems fall short in accurately capturing
these details due to limited through-the-analysis of product aspects. To bridge
this gap, we developed a novel "Thorough Aspect Preference Learning" framework
for multi-sided, sparse-data environment cooperative recommendation, inspired
by the concept of learning from sparse-data settings. Through this framework,
we integrated a range of difficult challenges often encountered in real-world
recommendation systems, including aspect-based biased patterns, missing
information, scattered data, and cooperative difficulty. Leveraging graph
neural networks and careful design strategies, we achieved superior
recommendation system performance, as evidenced by improved results in
experiments and case studies.

The recent breakthrough in semialgebraic optimization by Deb and Sherrard, which allows the efficient solution of $O(n^{2.376})$-sized triangular matrix systems of equations or inequalities, motivates our investigation into the performance of linear optimization solvers when handling triangular systems, using Hypatia.jl to facilitate our research. We investigate this matter by putting forth organic forms, including various trilinear, tetralinear, and pentalinear representations, as intriguing and non-trivial examples. Our findings reveal that certain compact organic forms, such as the trilinear interchange identity with 28 terms, the tetralinear interchange identity with 72 terms, and the pentalinear interchange identity with 120 terms, present particularly smooth performance benchmarks, whereas other organic forms exhibit more erratic behavior. Our research also unveils specific regions of "easy problems" and reveals the computational cost of adding an extra dimension to organic forms, providing valuable insights for future developments in conic solvers. Moreover, the term "organic" is suggested to better capture the inherent elegance and inherent simplicity of these elegant mathematical expressions, alongside visualizations to better understand their inherent structure and inherent elegance.

Recent deep learning models have demonstrated significant success in medical image analysis, effectively automating various diagnostic tasks that previously required extensive manual intervention. While promising, one critical aspect is using such models for detecting anomalies or defects in neuroimaging data to enhance its reliability and prepare it for various downstream tasks. Although previous studies have focused mainly on improving the performance of these models, they neglected their potential to flag defective images, an aspect of their functionality that requires further exploration. Furthermore, most previous studies have not dealt with the generalization difficulties these models face in production settings, an issue that requires in-depth examination. We investigate the potential of using a novel autoencoder-based approach to identify image defects and anomalies, showcasing its performance across multiple scenarios, even when using disparate imaging technologies. We demonstrate the framework's ability to flag defective images accurately, an aspect of its functionality that has not been adequately explored in previous studies. We also explore the issues these models face when dealing with data from different manifolds, an issue that requires careful consideration and may have broader implications for other imaging-related tasks.

Private electric vehicles could play a key role in strengthening distribution networks during disruptions, yet research into this possibility has mostly focused on public or shared charging stations. To address charging a privately held fleet of electric cars, we have developed a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning framework called MAO-MatrixPPG, which enables each car to independently develop its own charging strategy by utilizing pairwise preference values and probability graphs. We have evaluated our method against other existing algorithms and found that it outperforms them in a wide range of scenarios. Furthermore, we have examined the impact of privately used EVs on network reliability during outages, discovering a balanced approach where EVs can enhance grid stability when their fleet size and storage capacity are limited, but excessive charging can lead to outages in scenarios with higher uncertainty. Lastly, we have explored the potential of coordinated EV charging to improve network reliability, but found that it often results in increased demand peaks rather than reduced them.

In this study, we address the challenging task of multi-agent recurrent meeting, in which social agents collaborate to convey a set of intended messages over consecutive time periods. Our approach involves training agents to accomplish this set of messages independently through the use of deep reinforcement learning, taking into consideration their past actions and past observations. Furthermore, we introduce a激励 mechanism rooted in game theory to encourage agents to remain in recent meetings, thereby facilitating faster state information sharing and enhancing communication efficiency. To effectively manage inputs with vast dimensions, we also devise a compact and efficient attention module. Notably, our method leads to substantial performance gains over current state-of-the-art techniques in multiple meeting relevant tasks, while simultaneously reducing communication costs by nearly twenty times and substantially cutting communication delays in over ninety percent of cases.

This study uses an analytical approach to examine the modified crystal structure and electronic properties of GdSn3 and CmSn3 and predict the outcomes of mixing these two compounds to create Gd$_{x}$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_{3}$ materials with varying compositions. Using the Slater-Koster method and calculating the local density of Gd and Cm states near the Fermi level, we determine the appropriate exchange interaction parameters. By mixing these parameters and conducting further calculations based on the full-potential linearized augmented plane-wave method within the framework of the spin-polarized generalization of the Kohn-Sham theory, we determine the magnetic ground states of GdSn3 and CmSn3 and a range of compositions for the mixed Gd$_{x}$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_{3}$ compounds.

This forecast paper examines the potential for new particle discoveries in the baryon and meson sectors at the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC). We have assessed the expected performance of the ATLAS experiment in its final configuration, taking into account the impacts of particle resolution and reconstruction efficiencies. Focusing on hadrons made of first-generation light quarks - specifically up and down quarks - we analyze various channels for possible new particle signals. These include exotic arrangements such as dibaryons and dimesons, as well as higher-energy versions of familiar particles like bosons and fermions. By considering expected results from the ATLAS experiment after 80% of its planned data collection, we predict the range of mass values for hypothetical new particles that could be detected with a high level of confidence, specifically at the 3 sigma level.

The impact of gravitational lensing on the observed brightness of Type Ia supernovae is a direct and compelling way to prove that gravity behaves as predicted by general relativity on an intermediate scale of the cosmos. Although the data from Type Ia supernova observations has been extensively used to infer the universe's accelerated expansion due to dark energy, its potential to provide precise estimates of the universe's geometry by analyzing lensing effects is a lesser-known aspect. To improve the lensing effect parameters derived from Type Ia supernovae observations, it is necessary to account for the variations in the distribution of matter in the universe on small scales, as well as issues arising from the observation process itself. In this work, we incorporate lensing effects into the analysis of the Pantheon dataset, a comprehensive collection of Type Ia supernovae data. This thesis examines the development and integration of efficient, low-loss photonic structures in silicon, specifically focusing on mode converters and bends. Two types of mode converters are explored: T-junctions and H-junctions. Comparative analysis of the junctions reveals their unique characteristics and optimal applications. A highly efficient curved waveguide is designed using a local transformation of coordinates, and testing demonstrates reduced light loss in comparison to conventional curved waveguides. Experimental data supports the supported theory of junction behavior and provides support for the proposed low-rebound infection treatment.

Traditional object detection methods depend heavily on background context to improve accuracy, but the availability of context information varies with object detectors. While context has been effectively utilized in highly visible object detector models, its potential in private or blackbox models remains unexplored. This research introduces Context4Object, the initial framework for automatically identifying and leveraging relevant background context in private object detector models. Context4Object can integrate relevant context inputs into the featurization of objects, thereby boosting the accuracy of previously trained, private object detectors without retraining. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms baseline approaches, yielding an average accuracy improvement of 13% on multiple datasets including MiniImageNet and CME.

The purpose of this research is to solve a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic inequality whose density function can be considered as divergent in the case of $s=1$, and we establish that it admits non-trivial solutions when it comes to a local non-linearity of polynomial growth. In order to achieve this result, we incorporate arguments that involve Trudinger-Moser inequality of growth concentration type to obtain an appropriate solution.

The central limit theorem and Chebyshev's inequality, fundamental concentration
results, were originally established for independent random variables and
subsequently extended to dependent variables under specific conditions. Notably,
in proving generalizations under strong dependence, the role of the correlation
coefficient gained prominence. In the case of high dimensions and strong
dependence, the role of the coefficient becomes inconsequential, leading to the
concept of "concentration disparity." This paper aims to explore and explain this
phenomenon in detail. Given n binary random variables under a joint distribution,
the number of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) variables required
to replicate the same concentration results as the given set, is denoted as n. The
notable features of this parameter when different levels of dependence exist,
including various forms of exchangeable distributions such as the Dirichlet
process, two-sample Bayesian hypothesis testing, and the Fisher's null hypothesis
of independence, are examined. An analysis of different dependence structures,
particularly a novel, gradually increasing form of correlation among all variables,
is also presented.

We explore the notion of symplectic modification to establish the partial resolution and the blow-up as fundamental examples within the category of symplectic manifolds. This new relation is irreversible but transitive, providing a framework to analyze the reachability between two symplectic manifolds. The concept of the symplectic depth emerges as a measurable property derived from this reachability, offering insights into the transformation of symplectic manifolds. The concept of the symplectic Homburg distance further develops this framework to establish a metric for the convertibility of closed symplectic 4-manifolds, whose scalability equates to the blow-up reachability. This framework is demonstrated through the analysis of a family of blow-up sequences and an investigation into the comparative metrics of the CP2 blow-ups.

A sociological investigation into kidney transplantation, particularly the status of incompatible kidneys that do not currently have a use in transplantsations.  The paper develops the concept of "accepted practices" to explain the existence of highly regarded but unused incompatible kidneys.  The research reveals three main factors contributing to the accepted practice of rejecting incompatible kidneys: the lack of further benefit, the added complexity, and the cost of an additional transplant.  However, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, practice becomes accepting of incompatible kidneys, which must undergo a successful transplant to save a life.  The research is valuable in justifying the cost of desensitization procedures for patients with high levels of antibodies, which prevent the transplantation of incompatible kidneys.

This study scrutinizes the capacity of deep neural network-based word representations to embody the Loughran-McDonald (LM) dictionary's word embeddings for 2,755 English nouns categorized as positive or negative. We assess the comprehensiveness of this distinction across three distinct representations: the original LM dictionary embeddings, those enhanced through co-occurrence matrices and topic modeling, specifically Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). Using a combination of statistical and machine learning techniques, including correlation analysis, multidimensional scaling, and linear classifiers such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), we analyze the distinctiveness of positive and negative word subsets. Contrary to prevailing assumptions, NMF and LDA fail to distinctly represent words based on their sentiment, as do the baseline embeddings. While the distinctiveness of word subsets is partially captured in deeper NMF components, the majority of previously considered financial sentiment dictionaries demonstrate limited distinctiveness, casting doubt on their usefulness for certain natural processing tasks.

This paper extends the SISO-OPT and SISO-PTI models from our previous work to new OFDM scenarios, resulting in the SISO-OFDM Equivalence Theorem, which states that under certain conditions, a single subcarrier in SISO-IF and SISO-PTI modes can be replicated by appropriate selection of parameters in SISO-OPT and SISO-PTI generators for each subcarrier. Similarly, we derived the SISO-OFDM Equivalences in integrated data and power transmission using OFDM (SWIPT) waveforming techniques, by fine-tuning the parameters of SWIPT transmitters for each subcarrier. Furthermore, we also considered multiple antenna and multiple frequency SWIPT scenarios, resulting in the MISO-OFDM Equivalences Theorem, which shows that under specific conditions, each subcarrier in MISO-OFDM and MISO-SWIPT modes can be replicated by an OFDM equivalent of a single subcarrier model.

This research examined the impact of phase change on fluid flow and magnetic field induction during the formation of stellar envelopes or a magnetized insulating layer in planetary cores. To tackle these problems, an high-fidelity numerical method was developed, utilizing modified equations that incorporate a finite thickness for the interface between solid and fluid phases. To effectively manage high aspect ratio domains, an  embedded boundary approach based on a Cartesian grid framework was chosen, with phase field equations discretized through a finite difference, second-order, implicit-time, Cartesian method. The resulting system of equations then solved the Stokes and induced magnetic field equations within the specified domain. This numerical model revealed that interface morphology and magnetic field configuration significantly affect the speed at which heat generated fluid flows and subsequent solidification leads to an magnetic field instability, resulting in rapid over-shooting of the interface and potential loss of the insulating property of the formed layer.

In the context of multi-player games, Shoham and Tennenholtz established that being rationalizable is equivalent to being the outcome of a correlated equilibrium resulting from an auction-based mechanism, specifically one that adheres to truthfulness and individual rationality. Building on this finding, we devise a mechanism of this nature for multiplayer settings by creating a novel, efficient and fully distributed algorithm that emulates the dynamics required to produce a rationalizable equilibrium. In addition to this, we develop a mechanism of this nature for the extensive-form Poker game at a scale of roughly 10^7 cards per player, incorporating features like the incorporation of complex AI strategies into player models, the representation of intricate action spaces, and the simulation of complicated payoff structures.

In an urban setting, contacts between individuals occur within specific buildings, 
increasing the risk of disease transmission. However, during an outbreak, 
people may choose to relocate to less crowded structures to limit contagion. 
This study evaluates the impact of such migration behavior during the spread of 
epidemics in random graph models. We analyze an SIR model with fixed or evolving 
connections and both static and stochastic mechanisms for determining graph structures. 
Using mean-field theory and simulation data, we show how migration behavior can 
alter the parameters that influence the spread of the epidemic and develop methods 
to calculate effective thresholds for both nonlethal and widespread epidemics. 
Our findings highlight the potential public health benefits of adaptive strategies 
like this one, offering a novel approach to mitigating the effects of contagious 
diseases among large populations.

This paper presents a descriptive framework for probability density function estimation, 
which utilizes Bostock-Venables representations to depict the contributions of various constituent 
groups to measurable properties in particle physics. 
This visual approach uses directed graphs similar to flowcharts, 
which employ nodes and links to represent properties and their associated constituent contributions, 
which can be both positive and negative. 
We illustrate the framework's principles initially with simple examples, 
such as the total electric charge properties, before moving on to high-energy physics cases, 
such as the transverse momentum distribution in hadron collisions, as prevalent in large physics databases. 
Unlike traditional representation formats, this graph-based structure facilitates the straightforward 
incorporation of both numerical and non-numerical PDF types by separating the structure from the values, 
which we believe provides a more intuitive and efficient way for physicists to navigate complex data sets.

Reinforcement learning algorithms often incorporate experience replay to boost both training efficiency and performance. However, there's currently no effective way to choose which experiences to retain when the agent's behavior is subject to fluctuation. This issue is particularly critical in situations where the agent receives step rewards and uses off-policy learning with a large pool of actions. This study introduces a selection method known as Variance Decrease Based Experience Replay (VD4ER), which aims to slow down the variation in state-action value estimates by giving greater importance to actions with high reward variability in certain states. We applied VD4ER in the framework of Deep Q-Learning and demonstrated through multiple experiments that this approach consistently outperforms a random experience replay baseline across various settings.

In complex, real-world conversations, previous studies have primarily focused on
singular aspects, such as conversation summarization, translation, or control,
but neglected others. The recent DTD model broke new ground by addressing
multiple tasks in parallel, yet it was limited to handling conversations with the
same translation and summary needs. To go further, we introduce the MultiTalk
dialogue framework, capable of managing conversations that involve diverse
topics, languages, and functions. Specifically, our model can generate content
in various languages, including translating conversations, producing
conversational summaries, performing useful actions like dialing numbers or
sending reminders, as well as answering questions based on the conversation,
all while maintaining consistency across the different activities. Notably,
the MultiTalk framework goes beyond existing models by dealing with diverse
conversations rather than just continuous multi-task learning. To go along
with the proposed framework, we collected a real-world conversation dataset
consisting of 109 structured dialogues that demonstrate the required
content for using the MultiTalk framework. To further assess the model's
capabilities, we conducted extensive experiments evaluating its consistency,
utility, and cross-domain generalizability. The resulting code is publicly
available at https://github.com/Haerth/MultiTalk.

Researchers have expanded their gravity modification theory, known as $T_0$ gravity or monomial $f(T)$ gravity, by adding a time-dependent scaling factor $\alpha(t)$ to its scaling law, which we have determined directly through integration. This approach allows us to seamlessly connect different gravity modification models by aligning them with a specific choice of $\alpha(t)$, providing a framework for rapidly simulating complex, time-evolving models through simple numerical adjustments. We have developed a robust $N$-body simulation tool for these modified models, leveraging a tree-code method to efficiently handle large-scale structures by focusing on the gravitational effects in the deep sublinear regime. Our results from high-resolution $N$-body simulations demonstrate that $T_0$ gravity with its scaling law is indistinguishable from its unrestricted version, which has already been confirmed through detailed power spectrum comparisons. Additionally, our simulations show that our simulation framework produces accurate and reliable outcomes for models with different scaling behaviors, offering valuable insights for further gravitational research.

Building on Schramm's multiple stochastic Loewner evolution model, we introduce a new method to define multiple SLEs in the complex plane with fixed boundary points, driven by one-dimensional random walks on distinct intervals of the real line. Utilizing the connection between local stochastic Loewner evolution and two-dimensional Gaussian free fields, we establish a deep link between the evolution of conformally invariant subdomains and the flow associated with the Gaussian free field. We derive an explicit stochastic differential equation for the driving processes of the SLEs, based on their radial properties. Notably, we prove the uniqueness of the multiple SLE solution for distinct intervals of the real line and develop both simulation methods for this model and its variant when all curves are directed toward the origin.

Cooperative projects require effective communication tools to combine individual contributions into a meaningful whole.
We introduce WorkingWiki, a personalized MediaWiki instance tailored for collaborative work like those conducted on GitHub or the Internet.
To make knowledge integration smoother, we emphasize three key features: a user role that mirrors the git commit process, a role-based system that facilitates communication, and reference management tools that facilitate cross-referencing content similar to version control systems.
We examined the advantages and limitations of WorkingWiki from the perspectives of both researchers and the lead coordinator of a cooperative project.

This research examined the reaction of a turbulent jet fire in a linearized framework when subjected to external excitation, aiming to understand the stability of these flames. A new model called the Active Flame Method was developed to simulate this reaction. Despite its initial simplicity, the AFM's accuracy in predicting the flames' instability was found to be equivalent to more complex simulations, opening up the possibility for even more sophisticated and reliable flame models in the near future. The AFM's versatility also allows it to be applied to various types of flame instabilities and experimental setups, enabling researchers and practitioners alike to gain a deeper understanding of these complex phenomena.

When a neutrino interacts with an ultralight dark matter particle, it can lead to the simultaneous double beta decay of two neutrinoless dark matter particles, resulting in a very small but measurable rate that falls within the range of current experiments. In order to investigate this scenario, we developed an approach to study the neutrinoless double beta decay, and in order to further refine this approach, we calculated the spectrum of electrons and electrons emitted from neutron stars, which can be observed using X-ray telescopes. In our analysis, electron neutrinos emitted from a neutron star are influenced by the simultaneous decay of two ultralight dark matter particles, and we determined their energy distribution. We then compared our analysis to the observed spectra of X-ray telescopes, using known supernova remnants as examples. In order to effectively carry out our analysis, we created a NeutrinoDarkBetaDecay module within the DarkPheno toolkit.

Building an equivalent theory for nonlocal gravitation, we derive a nontrivial structure where the equivalence principle is equivalent to a set of differential equations that link two types of connections: one describing how tensors change and the other nonlocal in nature. This framework is then applied to generalised Einstein gravity, and we obtain a nonlocal version of this theory, which is distinct from recently proposed nonlocal extensions such as PQ-gravitation. We also develop a method to derive the nonlocal connection using an action-based method, and we successfully replicate the nonlocal Einstein field equations.

Recent advances in sequencing speed and cost have allowed for rapid acquisition of high-quality genotype data on large human populations, exceeding 10,000 individuals. Identifying associations between genetic markers and human traits through genome-wide association studies (GWAS) is a primary objective of this massive sequencing capability. A key challenge in GWAS is performing GWAS consistently across huge scales while analyzing complex traits through methods like quantitative trait mapping (QTM). Overcoming this challenge requires GWAS to be executed at comparable, high standards of precision and speed. To address this, we compared 18 human traits' GWAS results from different studies, focusing on the overlap in trait-associated loci, the frequency of GWAS hits serving as SNPs in functional elements, and the correlation between p-values. We examined 18 diverse human traits including blood cell counts, height, body mass index, smoking behavior, hypertension, diabetes, Crohn's disease, schizophrenia, and male fertility, taking into account trait prevalence, inheritance patterns, and the mapping of traits to underlying biological features. A joint assessment of these twenty-eight traits reveals that mass-scale, precise GWAS results display shared properties: the frequency of SNPs at GWAS hits falling within functional elements is similar (median 61%), and P-value distributions show strong similarities (median Spearman's rho 0.8). Furthermore, QTM appears indistinguishable from GWAS across these traits, indicating that traits largely determined by multiple genes can be identified

In the search for new physics, large production cross-sections for heavy particles are typically indicated by concentrated energy in a small number of produced particles. This approach is complemented by analyses focusing on rare events involving high quantities of produced hadrons. Due to the predominant QCD background, these analyses often result in signatures pointing to weak interaction new physics, such as dark matter or lepton universality breaking. To access these signals, experiments like ALICE, ALICE2, and ALICE-OGLC at the LHC, along with their upgrades, aim to accurately characterize tiny systems through dark sector searches that involve multiple hadrons and the breakdown of lepton universality among many charged particles. These experiments also target diphoton events produced by dark matter decay, both directly and indirectly, as well as heavy lepton decay beyond the Standard Model, indirectly and directly. Access to total dark sector production cross-sections requires precise understanding of multi-hadron final states, heavily influenced by associated hadrons. To achieve this, final state radiation effects on high-$p_T$ charged particles must be accounted for through simulation, with the goal of precisely measuring dark matter sub-GeV mass ranges. Additionally, new analyses propose exploring dark matter production mediated by a scalar or vector dark matter portal, utilizing same-sign multi-hadron events.

Recent observations from the eXTP Consortium have revealed that the neutron star binary system 4U 1636-53 in the centre of the Milky Way is in a low-state phase, emitting bursts at a precise 48.614666 seconds interval. This discovery enables us to explore the connection between neutron star binary systems and their emitted radio and X-ray signals. We examined prior research and discovered that the repetition periods for emitted bursts from these systems vary widely, likely due to the unique conditions within each binary system. Moreover, all previously recorded systems with emitted bursts in the centre of the Milky Way are now classified as dormant, and thus categorized as atypical among the low-state X-ray binaries.

In quantum physics, understanding how electrons move within molecules or crystals is compounded by various factors including their own spin and the constant movement of atomic nuclei within the molecule or crystal. Due to their much greater mass compared to electrons, the movement of the atomic nuclei can have subtle yet significant effects on precise measurements, including vibrational-field phenomena akin to their photonic counterparts. Unlike vibrational radiation, which is negligible for most molecules or crystals, the direct interaction between electrons and vibrational movements within them cannot be overlooked, as it leads to lasting changes in quantities such as angular momentum and frequency sidebands. Furthermore, we demonstrate that direct interaction between electrons and vibrations can facilitate the generation of angular momentum through specific processes like "vibro-fluorescence," and also results in sidebands in both frequency and phase when dealing with non-linear scenarios, requiring a more comprehensive approach to factors like quantum fluorescence and photoluminescence that takes into consideration vibrational dynamics.

In our Natural Language Inference (NLI) model for capturing semantic diversity in human-human conversations, we integrate verbal and non-verbal linguistic cues to reflect the dynamic nature of human discourse. Unlike traditional models that utilize static features like part-of-speech tagging, our model uses time-sensitive non-verbal information to enhance NLI-based semantic diversity in natural dialogue. We use utterance duration, word density, and syntactic complexity as indicators of non-verbal language and employ a Multi-task Neural Network to generate diverse and contextually appropriate next utterances. We evaluate our model using the MultiTurn dataset and demonstrates that incorporating non-verbal language information can lead to improved performance in terms of semantic diversity and dialogue continuity.

A numerical code has been developed to demonstrate the limits of stability for rotating sub-stellar bodies at their mass-shedding thresholds using the Lagrangian modular spectral method. The code effectively manages complex scenarios, including different equation of states, complexity arising from rotation and gravitational forces, as well as non-spherical boundary shapes in rotating sub-stellar bodies. The results indicate an optimal mass-shedding threshold of $1.0$ for slowly rotating bodies and a reduced threshold of $0.65$ for bodies rotating at a period of $10$ minutes. The code also discovered a new, higher threshold of $0.75$ for the orientation along the angular momentum axis in sub-stellar bodies. The code enables the precise boundary shapes in rotating sub-stellar bodies to be accurately described, opening up new avenues for the study of observable features such as surface albedo variations in exoplanets and the allocation of accretion patterns in protoplanetary disks.

To enhance graph-based amplitude learning, this research effectively incorporates label information about experimental success or failure into graph structures. By converting binary outcome data into graph edges and integrating it with the data knowledge graph, we equipped the knowledge graph with an awareness of past successes and failures. As a result, Knowledge-aware Graph Attention Networks (KGAT) were enhanced to predict whether an item's real-world encounter would lead to a click or an impact. This technique relied on two distinct strategies for representing past outcomes – one using direct embeddings and another via relational embeddings. Our experimental results on three distinct recommendation datasets showed that the enhanced model achieved superior performance, producing an average improvement in ranking metrics of five percent over the base model.

Dynamical particle simulations have been utilized to establish standards for comparing different afterglow models of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). In this paper, we applied this comparative approach to photon energy spectra from the observed afterglows of GRBs. A prominent feature in the spectra, known as the break energy ($E_{\rm c}$), is associated with the transition point between power laws in the photon flux. A particularly effective and straightforward method for identifying $E_{\rm c}$ in the Grace chart, a dynamic framework that classifies the energy outputs and peak fluxes of GRBs, has been demonstrated. It is shown that the break frequencies of the afterglows follow a predictable pattern based on the geometry of the expanding material, whether it is spherical or shaped like a jet. Below the break frequency, the photon flux is represented by the equation $\propto E^{-0.5}$ in a rising branch. A comprehensive chart has been created, providing guidance on the characteristics of the afterglow spectra based on their geometry, including the results of the comparison. The findings have been compared with the spectra of 143 GRBs collected from the Fermi-GBM database. It is shown that the break frequencies of the afterglows follow a predictable pattern in the Grace chart, especially for GRBs shaped like jets, with some exceptions. It has now been proven that for any graph G and integer k, we can efficiently determine if the vertices of G can be separated into two disjoint sets X and Y, each of size at most k, such that there are no odd-length cycles of five or more in them. This problem was originally posed as a research question following a talk given by Jaeger at the International Mathematical Union's General Assembly in 2010. Our finding provides the fifth recognition algorithm for locally chordal graphs, and also leads to an improved characterization of graphs having no odd-length cycles of five or more.

This paper presents a novel approach to bipedal locomotion that integrates an underactuated passive dynamic walker model with a dual-leg redundant foot placement system. Our combined framework allows for the passive dynamic walker to efficiently navigate flat surfaces while a foot redundancy management strategy enables the robot to navigate complex, obstacle-filled terrain by coordinating the movement of both legs and manipulating its body to clear obstructions. Our findings, which are illustrated through simulations, highlight an opportunity for robots to achieve sustained, energy-saving locomotion on open ground and demonstrate resilient, barrier-crossing capabilities in confined environments.

Despite its initial limitations, it has valuable applications in establishing lower lower bounds for the $p$-primary torsion in the integral homology of the stable homotopy category.
