Counterfactual phrases represent effective titles for articles in the field of natural language processing by providing information about what a particular sentence could have been to yield different outcomes. Researchers have been seeking difficult questions that large language models answer incorrectly, with the goal of improving their performance. This project involves collecting an extensive list of phrasal counterfactuals, with the help of an automated system, across various categories and complexities. This dataset comprises nearly seven thousand examples spanning simple substitutions to intricate causality transformations, with the aim of enhancing the performance of extensive language models. Results obtained on three models answerting three distinct questions indicate that our base line methods lead to significant improvements in performance, with the average accuracy increasing from 25.5% to 41.0% for Model 1, from 35.0% to 45.5% for Model 2, and from 55.0% to 60.5% for Model 3. These findings demonstrate that the field of NLP can benefit from investigating more intricate counterfactual relationships and that an automatic counterfactual generation method leads to significant performance improvements for the current manual approaches employed in the field.

Graphene epitaxy on sapphire has been successfully used to produce pure chemical composition in Heusler films, due to its ability to minimize interference patterns and increase reaction efficiency. A study focusing on Heusler film production on graphene and direct epitaxy surfaces has analyzed the influence of pinhole sites, which do not adhere to strict reaction rules but instead follow similar physical laws to other surface phenomena, resulting in contamination and reduced performance. As the number of Heusler pinhole sites grows, particularly during extended film production, it becomes increasingly difficult for films to achieve desired characteristics, as the heusler phases begin to overtake the [111] oriented graphene surfaces. A optimal approach is to balance the number of Heusler pinhole sites by using temporary surfaces that adhere to similar reaction rules, allowing for the creation of multilayered structures with diverse properties. Using this approach, researchers created multilayered structures consisting of different Heusler phases and found that they exhibited superior electrical properties compared to single-phase films.

Recently, Grobler et al. introduced the concept of $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes and identified four distinct rank-related parameters: rank, co-rank, reduced rank, and nullity. This study establishes the relationship between these parameters, demonstrating that any $n$-ary $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear code's parameters can be precisely described using four integers that satisfy specific inequalities. Moreover, it is proven that any such code can be equivalently represented as the sum of four independent components: a primary code of length $n$ over $\mathbb{Z}_p$, an ideal within a secondary code of length $n$ over $\mathbb{Z}_p$, along with two additional independent components of lengths $n$ over $\mathbb{Z}_p$. The study provides several examples to further clarify these concepts.

Supervised learning models trained on single-label classification often suffer from performance degradation when applied to multi-label classification scenarios, due to the distinct characteristics of multi-label data. We've discovered that such data can be further categorized into single-label and multi-label instances, and that cross-situation generalization is limited by the absence of relevant training data for one of the categories. To bridge this gap, we propose Label Instances Extraction (LIE), a novel framework that leverages underrepresented data from the dataset with abundant labeled information. By curating diverse and informative samples, LIE enhances the effectiveness of multi-label data under a single-label setting. Our method has been evaluated on eight widely-used datasets, demonstrating consistent multi-label and joint setting performance improvements.

This 2-categorical abstracted version of the Robinson correspondence stands out as a meaningful connection, linking the direct relationship between grammars and formal languages with the classical parser-generator link. The original discovery was made by B. Robinson in 1965, establishing a one-to-one mapping between Chomsky grammars and deterministic finite automata, along with their transition and yield relations. In 2014, D. Penner expanded on this work, interpreting the automata as part of the complete structure and demonstrating the same type of connection that initially applies to context-free grammars, which are a subset of the languages defined by Chomsky's type 2 framework. Using this 2-categorical perspective, multiple aspects of the Grammars-Automata relationship and the Parser-Generator relationship can be seen as instances of the same fundamental principle.

The nature of energy sources powering high-luminosity galaxies is an area of scientific interest.
The higher-energy signals from spiral galaxies, specifically in the gamma-ray spectrum, are not well understood.
By applying the principles of plasma physics to galaxy components, two mechanisms were identified that could contribute to gamma-ray signals: magnetic reconnection occurring within the galactic disk and acceleration of particles by the magnetic fields of the galactic disk.
These theories indicate that gamma-ray signals should be produced when the magnetic fields of the disk reach a certain strength and intensity.
However, past studies using standard galaxy models failed to detect the expected gamma-ray signals due to the long duration of particle particle interactions.
When magnetically captured galaxies are considered, the models predict that gamma-ray signals would be produced at lower energies and detectable from nearby galaxies such as Andromeda (M31).
When gamma-ray observations from M31 are compared to the model predictions, the data are found to be comparable to the expected signals from magnetic capture, and this process may be responsible for the overall gamma-ray emission from M31.

Heart disease remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide, and apical heart sounds are critical indicators for detecting and diagnosing cardiac disorders.  To effectively identify heart abnormalities, accurate and timely heart sound diagnosis is essential.  However, obtaining high-quality heart sounds in real-world settings is often complicated by various factors, including patient discomfort, difficulty in placing the stethoscope correctly, and external noises like phone rings, alarms, and other disturbances.  These issues result in heart sounds that are noisy and distorted, posing a significant obstacle to heart sound diagnosis.  In this study, we address the issue of diagnosing heart sounds with external noise interference and heart sounds that undergo frequency shifting and time stretching.  To accomplish this, we developed a novel heart sound classification model capable of categorizing normal heart sounds, those with added noise, and those that are stretched or shifted, into three classes.  Our proposed deep learning framework combines predictive models, including noise inversion and inverse transformations, to remove external sounds and reverse transformations, and then employs a neural network to classify the heart sounds into three categories based on their characteristics.  To evaluate the proposed method, we used a dataset of heart sounds and were able to successfully classify normal heart sounds, those with added noise, and those that are stretched or shifted, into three classes.  To further demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, we compared its results with those of state-of-the-art deep learning models and found that our approach yielded better performance in heart sound classification tasks.

The rapid expansion of cloud computing and wearable technology has created significant potential for remote healthcare. Nevertheless, gathering high-quality health data on a large scale remains a challenge due to privacy concerns associated with sharing personal data. In the FedHealth project, we are investigating a federated learning method that allows wearable devices to provide accurate health predictions without compromising user privacy. FedHealth combines the advantages of federated learning and transfer knowledge in a novel framework. It leverages a transfer knowledge structure to bridge the gap between simple devices with limited sensors and powerful servers, enabling more effective model training. Furthermore, a knowledge distillation approach is used between devices to enhance collaboration and knowledge exchange. Experiments conducted with real-world data from wearables demonstrate the effectiveness of FedHealth in combining the benefits of transfer knowledge and federated learning for large-scale wearable data collection.

This paper examines the relationship between two portfolio management issues - portfolio enhancement through higher moments optimization and the development of robust portfolios via data noise resistance optimization. In recent years, various higher moments optimization approaches have been introduced, including the focus on the covariance hypothesis, and a new, underexplored connection is presented in this work, centered around the efficient frontier. To establish this new link, the efficient frontier is re-examined, and it is demonstrated that portfolios positioned at its extremities inherently incorporate an implicit efficient frontier, which can be utilized to identify the most resilient parameters in the moments optimization framework. Furthermore, it is established that the mid-point of the extreme portfolios corresponds to a portfolio selected with an implicit robust optimization framework, utilizing the Least Shrinkage and Generalized Cross Validation method. These findings can be applied to determine the most stable weights within the efficient frontier, and to select the most reliable parameters in the moments optimization framework.

This text is virtually identical to the abstract, which can be described as follows: A replication study by a team led by Drude Peters (University of Washington) and his researchers aims to match the results achieved by another group (named R1). The original study included 16 experiments designed to accomplish various goals, such as enhancing the efficiency of package management systems, optimizing installation processes for large suites of software, and exploring methods for automatically generating and formulating software hypotheses. To replicate the findings, the team ran all 16 experiments on two platforms, using an existing package of Python tools developed by the same group that created the results they aim to replicate. The study employed the same design frameworks and statistical analysis methods as the original research. Ultimately, the team succeeded in replicating most key findings of the initial research within one month.

Consider a T-varying cost control problem, in which the cost function can either increase or decrease at most T times. The problem seeks to minimize the final cost in a system evolving as a continuous path. I aim to extend the results from a prior study, where an optimal solution existed for steps costs (costs that can only change from one state to another), allowing the system to change states a maximum of 2^(2T) - 1 times over the time interval (0,1), or increase or decrease at most T times respectively. Nevertheless, with the option of bounds, even when the cost functions increase or decrease sequentially, the final number of necessary jumps to switch intervals grows exponentially, making the problem impractical for higher values of T.

In an attempt to address the low rate of neutral-current interactions observed in neutron beta decay, we analyzed a specific scenario where two types of leptoquarks, belonging to the scalar $\bar{3}_1$ representation, were produced within the Large Hadron Collider. By calculating both the leading-order and next-to-leading-order radiative corrections to their mutual scattering process, we determined the leading leptoquark type conversion cross-section, specifically the charged interaction that contributes to scalar currents. To leptoquark mass constraints, there must be sufficient space for a pair of leptoquarks of opposite charge to be produced at 8 TeV, which implies an upper limit of 46 GeV for the leptoquark mass. Notably, this leptoquark pair production scenario remains undetected in LHC data as of 13 TeV and 3.2 TeV with 11.9 and 0.8 nb of luminosity respectively.

Observing excitation temperatures in the low-energy interstellar radiation has long been challenging, especially with a chemical species whose first energy state is separated by more than 3 times the temperature of the cosmic microwave background. Although the exact mechanism for line emission in atomic carbon remains uncertain, it is hypothesized that non-thermal velocity distributions, resulting from the subthermal population of higher energy states, may play a key role. By combining radiative transfer and non-equilibrium statistical analysis methods, we examined the conditions required for atomic carbon lines to emerge in star-forming regions, photon-dominated regions, and dwarf galaxies. If our hypothesis holds, conditions in regions with enhanced molecular gas by a factor of 10 and in dwarf galaxies may lead to non-thermal velocity distributions and broad line profiles with full width at zero intensity values of several kilometers per second and several hundred kilometers per second, respectively. Additionally, we developed new formulas to estimate full width at zero intensity values based on velocity distributions and magnetic field values. We also proposed using line profiles to detect non-equilibrium conditions, high-density molecular gas, and suppressed star formation in galaxies and suggested leveraging line profiles and ratios to determine the atomic carbon reservoir's contribution to the total mass movement in galaxies.

Imagine a binary code consisting of multiple copies of a high-dimensional vector, where each dimension represents a unique value from 1 to n, and the values are arranged in ascending order. This code is called a sorted permutation, and we can think of it as a reference or "ground truth." Now, if we're given another set of $f(n)$ scrambled permutations and asked to rebuild the sorted permutation, we're facing a reconstruction challenge. To measure the discrepancy between the original and reconstructed permutations, we use a discrepancy metric known as the Hamming distance. If we use a standard majority vote to reconstruct the sorted permutation, we find that it accurately recreates each element of the original permutation if the number of scrambled permutations grows linearly with n. But as we want to create code with exponentially large capacity, new methods are necessary to improve efficiency. Using techniques such as locality correcting codes and error correcting codes, we can use quadratic, near-optimal, and polylogarithmic functions to accurately reconstruct the sorted permutation with a low probability of discrepancy.

As Pulsar Timing Array experiments progress with more sensitive data, potentially detecting gravitational waves from supermassive black hole merges and binaries, the likelihood of detecting non-circular (eccentric) signals will rise. The eccentricity of these binaries, however, complicates their analysis and theoretical modeling, requiring lengthy numerical relativistic simulations that are computationally expensive to generate and interpolate for efficient timing data comparison. In this study, we present a method to create high-fidelity, interpolable models of non-circular binary signals, even for high eccentricity cases, based on nearly exact full-waveform calculations. Our model achieves sub-percent accuracy, processes millions of pulsar observations per second on a standard computer, and comes with associated quality control metrics and guidance charts to evaluate signal fidelity and determine the necessary computational expenses for generating high-precision interpolations.

In 1991, Hammersley characterized the stochastic growth of a one-dimensional array of zeros and ones, where a zero adjacent to a one moves to its left with a specific probability $p$, otherwise it grows with adjacent ones on both sides. This model is commonly referred to as the asymmetric simple exclusion process when it is viewed from the perspective of the particles (zeros and ones switch roles). This paper introduces the ASEP velocity procedure as a dynamic extension of the associated data process, where each particle is assigned to a velocity based on its local surroundings. It is demonstrated that this process is closely related to the asymmetric simple exclusion process. Additionally, we establish that certain equilibria of a known family of stochastic differential equations can be found within the ASEP velocity procedure's framework.

Comprehensive epidemietic models have been successfully employed to analyze and manage epidemics over recent decades. Despite diverse approaches, these models have demonstrated common underlying structures, now utilized in analyzing the ongoing COVID-19 outbreak, with models being compared and contrasted in this review. Utilizing the distinctions between compartmental and individual-based frameworks, as well as fixed and evolving parameter sets, a unified classification system is established, providing a consolidated understanding of existing methodologies and their relevance to public health policy, with models being directly applied to the COVID-19 outbreak and their limitations and complexities being explored in this review.

Recently, new techniques for creating and manipulating spin-polarized cold atomic gases have been developed, which rely on three-body recombination. In a new model, three particles in an ultracold atomic gas, whose spins are polarization-transfer type and governed by short-range two-body interactions, can be described effectively by a three-body problem with residual interactions decaying at a rate of $1/a^3$. When these interactions reach a peak, they can cause both repulsive and attractive behaviors, which can hinder or enhance three-body processes, respectively, and have been observed to be universal and scalar, and thus, cannot be affected by external traps that influence atomic gases with contact interactions that vary with length. The influence of these three-body processes on the dynamics and the equilibrium state of the population of an arbitrary atomic molecule condensate formed in a specific length dimension has been studied in this report.

B-tree structures are an effective method for managing hierarchical and informational
aspects within DNA storage systems. Nevertheless, traditional B-tree algorithms
struggle with certain limitations, including the vast size of pointers in relation
to data addresses, bottlenecks during the synthesis and sequencing of DNA, which
impede the realisation of battery-powered electronics, leading to difficulty in
decoding entry addresses, among other issues. Furthermore, the current B-tree
methods fall short of optimising the layout of DNA storage entries to maximise
the similarity of sequences and minimise the locations where entries are situated
to maximise the overlap of storage locations. An improved battery-operated
B-tree structure is presented to address the above-mentioned limitations by
utilising the inherent hierarchy and informational properties of battery-powered
electronics-based DNA technology. The novel structure employs the inherent
binary nature of DNA addresses for hierarchical organisation, takes into
account the beginning location of storage entries for informational organisation,
and implements short addresses to take advantage of the inherent binary nature
of DNA technology for enhanced decoding entry addresses. Additionally, the
proposed structure considers the layout of storage entries to enhance the
similarity of sequences and the overlap of addresses location. Through
benchmarked comparisons, the proposed battery-operated B-tree structure is found
to outperform conventional B-tree structures in terms of synthesis, sequencing,
and retrieval operations in DNA technology.

The complex nature of differential equations poses a challenge in developing an efficient and user-friendly toolkit for various applications. This study proposes a novel approach to addressing the shallow water equations by incorporating a neural operator trained on high-fidelity data. By employing the DeepONet architecture, we achieve rapid solutions to a wide range of initial conditions and boundary conditions, as well as variable channel geometries. Our experiments demonstrate the neural operator's versatility, enabling it to handle changing geometries, boundary conditions, and variable geophysical parameters without altering the underlying framework. Moreover, we illustrate the benefits of this approach in a real-world application, such as predicting river water levels within seconds compared to traditional numerical methods which take several minutes. This study highlights the potential of machine learning techniques to provide a powerful and adaptable tool for solving differential equations in different contexts.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure settings to balance bright areas and dark regions in an image. While professional cameras allow manual settings, most consumer smartphones automatically determine the exposure brackets and blend images using simple methods, resulting in lower quality than desired. This research develops a comprehensive framework for enhancing high-dynamic-range mobile imagery, beginning with an optimal number of images and total combined range that considers both the camera's capabilities and the content's characteristics. Further, several content-aware image fusion techniques are explored and compared, including a novel hybrid approach that combines matrix decomposition and optimization, demonstrating significant improvements over existing methods.

Deep neural networks have significantly advanced in performance through the use of heuristics and empirical methods. However, they lack mathematical guarantees regarding performance and reliability. Causal machine learning aims to address this issue by enabling algorithms to make reasonable predictions and generalizations under new scenarios, even when faced with distributional shifts. This approach represents a progress from purely empirical models to ones with theoretical reliability, explicability, and robustness, while incorporating the concept of causality into neural network architecture and training procedures. This review explores the causal framework for machine learning, beginning with an introduction to structural equation modeling and the do-calculus, and proceeds to discuss research integrating these methods with deep learning, covering applications in inference, selection, and adjustment, as well as variations using generative models and generative adversarial networks, and discusses potential potential research directions.

Specifically, we establish the following result: given two transverse lagrangian submanifolds $L$ and $L'$ within the symplectization of a contact structure on a manifold with the homotopy type of $S^2$, if $L$ and $L'$ can be separated by all b-principles within the given contact structure, then they can also be separated by the symplectic caput principle within the same structure. However, we provide a series of examples demonstrating that in certain scenarios, contact-specific versions of the symplectic $h$-principle fail to hold, despite $L$ and $L'$ being separable by the symplectic caput principle. These exceptions indicate that the symplectic caput principle holds in the broader category of symplectizations, even though it does not necessarily imply that the inverse is true in the context of contact structures.

Understanding the mechanical behavior of the heart on a micro level remains a
multilevel challenge whose solution requires efficient numerical methods to
account for varying time and length scales within the heart. Traditional finite
element solvers struggle to manage these scales, necessitating innovative
preconditioners that can provide a robust, scalable alternative to these methods.
This study explores multilevel preconditioners derived from the mixed reformulation
of elasticity, comparing two variants based on fluid-elastic interaction
preconditioning. By examining two distinct models of the heart, this study
compares these variants and investigates their reaction to changes in time and
length scales in a unified framework. Both variants show comparable
performance and this multilevel preconditioner offers an efficient, multiscale
numerical solver for cardiac mechanics and other mechanical problems. This study's
findings indicate that multiple processors can be used to simulate the heart's
mechanics without sacrificing accuracy or scalability.

This study focuses on modeling the unique diffusion process observed in non-equilibrium conditions, where mean squared displacement grows at a rate between linear and quadratic growth. To achieve this, we developed a stochastic framework that incorporates fluctuating properties of a material's permeability. These materials consist of many compartments with varying sizes and levels of connectivity, and we modeled their impact on particle diffusion using an approach based on continuous time random walks. By integrating numerous individual simulations, we accounted for the diverse structures within the material's framework. Our results indicate that such hidden variables can generate the observed diffusion behavior, and as our scenario parameters change, we were able to reproduce the full spectrum of diffusion types from linear to quadratic growth. Additionally, our model can also describe super-diffusion with growth rates exceeding unity due to specific structural characteristics, and our framework is directly applicable to real-world materials and experimental data.

A mathematical model is developed to understand the optical properties of a resonator near a waveguide, taking into consideration both linear and Kerr nonlinear properties. A key aspect of this model involves modeling the optical fields using a combination of real and imaginary coefficients to represent the amplitude and phase of the light. Furthermore, a perturbation approach is used to obtain precise expressions for coupling coefficients that describe energy transfer between the resonator and waveguide modes. It is shown that a resonance formed by a waveguide mode and a resonator mode results in a change in phase of the transmitted light, with the phase shift depending on the optical power, characteristic of a phase transition. The model provides a comprehensive understanding of interactions between resonator and waveguide modes and can be applied to design optical devices based on phase shifts induced by nonlinearity.

Chaotic flow simulations offer a framework to forecast and manage real-world turbulent flows, yet they demand high-resolution data, making data acquisition difficult due to its dense data requirements. A new method using deep learning techniques, specifically a style transfer algorithm, restores low-resolution chaotic flow data to high-resolution, across various Reynolds numbers. This method relies on opposing networks to counteract resolution effects and an adversarial style transfer framework to integrate the opposing results, effectively combining the training benefits of both methods. This approach enables the restoration of accurate flow details and structural information from low-resolution data, providing a more precise and efficient way to study fluid dynamics and flow behavior for research purposes.

DL models' growing use in critical applications calls for improved robustness evaluation, 
which our new framework, L2Explorer, addresses. Inspired by reinforcement learning, 
L2Explorer provides an open-source and comprehensive platform for iterative 
improvements, featuring modular designs that facilitate the integration of novel 
experiments. Key components of L2Explorer include specialized explorers for 
navigate complex input spaces, a diverse dataset of demonstration examples, 
automated testing frameworks with modular designs, 
which the project's contributors found particularly valuable. 
Showcasing its versatility, L2Explorer has been utilized for evaluating various 
models including supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and adaptive models, 
as demonstrated in our initial applications focused on intrusion detection systems. 
By promoting standardization and generalization in robustness evaluation, 
L2Explorer fills an important gap in frameworks like GLUE and SuperGLUE, 
which it builds upon and extends.

In this work, we introduce a new method for analyzing and improving declarative programs using the tube framework, specifically tailored for specifications written with the CHARDIE method and represented as chains of equalities. To achieve this, the tube framework utilizes Choco and Chain. Choco, a change operator, enables the identification of data changes that occur between when a chain of equalities is given and when an expected outcome is not met. On the other hand, Chain, a learning component, extracts rules from these discrepancies in the form of logical implications. Chain has the ability to extract rants (negative examples) from system execution and replays traces (positive examples) to facilitate inference. To support the reconstruction of scenarios for rant generation and trace replay, Chain employs a model based on streams, which also provides an exploratory feature to generate new instances by combining replay and rant generation. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we have integrated Chain into the Choco framework and presented case studies involving the ChA$^{2}$D compilations. These case studies highlight how we can utilize Chain to analyze compiled specifications for issues such as non-existent solutions, incorrect solutions, and under-constrained problems, and generate learning rules in the form of implications.

Accurate sentiment evaluation is essential for establishing a person's online reputation and guiding reliable recommendations in various recommendation systems and social media platforms. This issue is particularly complex across different languages due to the lack of available data and the diverse nature of internet texts that contain various sentiment labels in multiple languages. To effectively analyze multilingual sentiment on a large scale, it is necessary to develop a framework for assessing recommendations and guiding them in a multilingual setting. Studies indicate that data from ICU installations can predict future outcomes effectively. An intriguing hypothesis suggests that whether an individual is admitted to an ICU may be evident as early as during an X-ray scan, potentially due to specific physiological conditions, such as the need for oxygen support, which could be linked to the presence of severe pneumonia depicted in the X-ray images. To explore this hypothesis, we compared the performance of a machine learning model trained to distinguish between COVID-19 patients requiring ICU admission and those who do not, using X-ray images. However, our results did not support this hypothesis, likely because of the limited size of the dataset used in the study, which comprised only 44 images of patients admitted to an ICU and 440 of patients who do not require ICU admission. We believe that a comprehensive model can be created which incorporates X-ray images, leveraging physiological cues depicted within, to signal patients requiring ICU admission, but this requires a substantial dataset, possibly augmented through techniques like transfer learning, to achieve accurate results.

The work in this paper extends the concept of a principal bundle over a simplicial space, establishing the conjuacy normal form for a simplicial group. A distinct characterization of discrete subgroups within these complexes is also proposed. Furthermore, a correspondence is proven between certain simplicial bundle structures and subgroups that satisfy specific criteria, effectively replicating the results of a previous study by Dyer and Canterbury in 1951 for standard simplicial groups.

This paper addresses the issue of erroneous positives in Visual Association Detection (VAD).  Such occurrences, where spurious connections between objects are learned, are a frequent issue in object detection and significantly hinder the applicability of VAD tasks.  Although objects' bounding boxes are independent given their identities in theory, ambiguous features, difficult backgrounds, and imperfect detectors often result in erroneous associations.  To mitigate this issue, our proposed method, Object Evidence VAD (OE-VAD), calculates the logit for each object to classify its existence in the particular scene.  This approach is straightforward and does not require any additional training stages or network modifications compared to existing methods, achieving superior results in our experiments.  Our data shows that OE-VAD achieves an average improvement of 11% in VAD metrics and 3% in association classification, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing visual association detection reliability.
